h1: Planning a brewpub for seasonal demand
title: Planning a Brewpub for Seasonal Demand | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan a brewpub around seasonal demand: read your own sales pattern, match brewing to it, flex staff and stock and protect cash in slow months.
teaser: Some months the room is full and some months it is not. Plan the year, not the week.
standfirst: Brewpub demand moves with weather, festivals and school holidays. This guide shows how to read your own pattern and plan brewing, staff and cash around it.
sections:
Almost every brewpub has busy months and slow ones. The pattern depends on the city, the site and the customers, so no general rule fits. A rooftop may fill in the cooler months and empty in the monsoon. A site near offices may dip during school holidays. What matters is your pattern, read from your own data.

Treat the seasonal curve as an input to every plan: brewing volumes, staffing, stock, marketing and cash.

Pull monthly sales for at least a year, split into beer, food and other. Divide each month by the average month of the year to get an index. A month at 1.3 is 30 per cent above average. A month at 0.7 is 30 per cent below. Look at weekdays and weekends separately.

If you are new, you have no data. Ask nearby venues, watch footfall and plan conservatively. Then record everything so next year's plan is better.

Beer does not keep forever, so brewing for the busy month means starting weeks earlier. A lager needs several weeks in tank, an ale less. Work back from the first busy day. Fermenters are your constraint: if two months of demand arrive in one, you need free tank space beforehand.

In the slow months, use the spare tanks. Brew the seasonal specials, trial new recipes or make beer for kegs to sell elsewhere. Our guide to contract brewing for the host covers selling spare tank time.

Hypothetical numbers in currency units. A brewpub sells 4,000 litres a month on average. Its busiest month runs at index 1.4, so 5,600 litres. Its slowest runs at 0.6, or 2,400 litres. With a contribution of 80 per litre and fixed costs of 250,000 a month, the busy month earns 448,000 of contribution and makes 198,000 profit. The slow month earns 192,000 and loses 58,000.

A brewpub that budgets on the average sees a comfortable 70,000 a month profit (4,000 x 80 less 250,000). It will feel rich in the busy month, then be short in the slow one. The fix is to hold back the surplus, so the slow month is already paid for.

Staff are the biggest controllable cost. Use a mix of core team and flexible hours. Cross-train people so a server can help in the kitchen. Order food in smaller, more frequent lots in the slow months to reduce waste. Hold less finished beer when you know sales will drop. Plan holidays and maintenance in the slow months, when the cost of closing a tank is lowest. Talk to your suppliers too. A supplier who knows your peak months can hold stock or agree a delivery schedule. That one conversation can cut the amount of cash tied up before the rush.

Slow months suit events that bring in a different crowd: tastings, food pairings, private bookings, a quiz night, a brewer's table. Keep them responsible and open to people who do not drink. Never run promotions that push people to drink more, such as unlimited offers. Quieter months are better used to build loyalty with regulars through a members' tasting or a small brewing day, so the customer who visits in July is the one who tells friends in October. Our guide on which of your beers make money helps choose what to brew and promote. Offer a good non-alcoholic option in every season. Test one idea at a time and record the result, so by next year you know which events earned their cost. A quiz night that fills ten tables on a Tuesday is useful. One that fills two is a favour to the staff.

The simplest protection is a reserve: set aside part of the busy-month surplus for the slow months. Build the seasonal curve into your 12-month cash flow. If you rely on a loan, make sure the instalment dates and any seasonal facility match your pattern. The course below teaches you to model the year with the curve built in.
faqs: How do I find my seasonal pattern?
Take monthly sales for at least a year and compare each month with the average. If you are new, watch footfall and ask nearby venues.
Should I brew less in slow months?
Not necessarily. Use spare tank time for seasonal beers, trials or kegs for other channels. Watch cash and shelf life.
How do I keep staff in slow months?
Use a core team plus flexible hours. Cross-train so people can cover several roles.
Is seasonality the same in every city?
No. It depends on weather, local events and the customer mix. Read your own data.
